## Why Captions Aren't Enough for Deaf People
URL: https://www.talksign.co/blog/why-captions-arent-enough
Published: 3 Sep 2026 | Category: Community | Author: Edidiong Ekong, CEO and Founder of Talksign

We often think language is just words. But for Deaf people, communication is much more than that. AI needs to understand this difference to truly help everyone.

Most of the time, when something isn't accessible, it's not because the information isn't there. It's because we think showing information is the same as making sure someone understands it. For example, a meeting might have live captions, and people say it's accessible. These things are helpful, but they both assume that language is only about words, and that showing someone words means they are part of the conversation.
 This idea isn't always true, and the numbers show a big problem. The World Health Organization says that over 430 million people (more than 5% of the world) need help with hearing loss. This number is expected to grow to over 700 million by 2050. Not helping with hearing loss costs the world almost $1 trillion each year. In Africa alone, about 40 million people have hearing loss. Captions and interpreters only reach a small part of these people, and usually, they only work one way.
 The hidden idea
 Technology for accessibility has always been limited by what AI can do. First, we had written words because speech could be turned into text. Then, screen readers turned text into spoken words because text fit easily into AI systems. Each new tool made us think the same way that language is a line of words, one after another, and meaning comes from these words in order and this has influenced the way modern AI language models are built as they focus on words in a sequence.
 Sign languages are not like a line of words. They are not just spoken words made with hands. They are independent natural languages with their own grammar, using hands, face, and body simultaneously to convey meaning. For example, in American Sign Language (ASL), a raised eyebrow can turn a sentence into a question; removing that signal (as plain captions do) can change the meaning entirely. A person signing shows hand shape, movement, facial expression, eye direction, and body position all at the same time, carefully timed. If you try to put all of that into captions, you don't just lose a little bit of information. You lose a whole way of communicating, because captions force something that isn't linear into a linear format. This is a problem with how we try to show the language, not a flaw in captions themselves. That's why Talksign treats each sign language as its own language to translate, not just a different version of another. For example, ASL and British Sign Language (BSL) are completely different, even though both countries speak English. If you try to use an ASL model with British words, BSL users will immediately know it's wrong.
 Here are some key ways sign languages work:
 Simultaneous channels: A single sign can combine several components (hand shape, movement, location, orientation) plus facial expression and body posture.
 Spatial grammar: Signers use the 3D space around them to show subjects, objects, or time. For instance, ASL often uses a “topic-comment” structure by placing a topic sign in space then a comment (e.g., signing STORE followed by I GO to mean “I’m going to the store”).
 Non-manual markers: Facial movements (eyebrows, mouth, head tilt) are part of the grammar, not just emotion. Without them, a signed sentence can be incomplete or ambiguous.
 Accessibility became about checklist
 For many businesses, accessibility is checked by audits, lists of requirements, and legal rules. These have helped a lot, but they often care more about what can be measured than how well people actually communicate. For example, they ask: Were captions there? Was a written copy made? Did an interpreter show up? These questions check if a service was provided, not if people actually understood each other. A company can follow all the rules and still have Deaf employees who can't understand meetings, Deaf patients who can't explain their symptoms, or Deaf customers who can't complain.
 Imagine a Deaf student watching a lecture video. The speaker’s tone rises in excitement, but captions just show “That was unexpected.” on screen. The student’s sign language would normally convey surprise or sarcasm through eyebrow raises and a change in pace, information lost in captions. A company meeting with captions may still feel confusing for Deaf attendees if jokes, sarcasm, or detailed questions aren’t fully captured.
 This problem is clear even when a lot of money is spent on accessibility. For example, FIFA will provide sign language interpreters for every game at the 2026 World Cup. This is the first time they've done this for a whole tournament. The interpreters don't just repeat what the commentators say; they also show the sounds of the whistles, the crowd, and the mood that a scoreboard can't show. This is a real step forward but FIFA itself says that the interpretation won't always match the action perfectly because it's live and done by humans for billions of viewers. Fans can see what the stadium feels like, but they still can't communicate back or be understood by the person next to them. For example, a Deaf fan might sign excitement to a hearing friend after a goal, but without an interpreter that friend hears nothing. Big sports events get this kind of help because they are important. Smaller events, like an away game or a local final, usually don't, because professional sign language interpreters often cost $75 to $125 an hour. This means accessibility is only given when an organization decides it's important enough to pay for.
 Why AI struggles with sign language
 Big AI models learn how words connect in a line as a sequence, no matter the spoken language. Sign languages, however, use many different ways to communicate at once. If you take away the facial expression from a sign, you can change its grammar. If you ignore where the sign is in space, you lose how it refers to things. If you remove the movement, you lose information about time. This is more like a problem for robotics or computer vision (how AI sees) than for regular language programs. Just making the AI bigger won't fix this; the way it's built needs to be right. As researchers Shakib Yazdani, Yasser Hamidullah, Cristina España-Bonet, Eleftherios Avramidis, and Josef van Genabith note in their paper, A Critical Study of Automatic Evaluation in Sign Language Translation , “Sign languages are highly expressive visual languages that convey meaning through hand signs, facial expressions, mouthings, and body posture.” Facial expression and timing are parts of sign language grammar. An AI that reduces everything to a text string will discard these crucial parts.
 For instance, an ASL signing avatar with a neutral face (no eyebrow or mouth movement) produces an ungrammatical message, like speaking in a flat monotone when emotion is needed. A simple ASL sentence for “He was here” might use a sign for HE, plus a quick head turn or shoulder raise to indicate past tense. If we only caption it as “He was here,” we miss that body cue showing when it happened. Likewise, a Deaf user asking “Are you going?” in ASL would sign the verb GO while raising eyebrows to mark a yes/no question. Captions can’t easily show the raised eyebrows.
 This is why we created Echo, our AI model that turns speech into sign. The easy way would be to turn speech into text, and then text into sign. But this doesn't work because the feeling and rhythm of speech (prosody) are lost when it's first turned into text. You can't get it back later, even though prosody should guide how the face and body move in sign language. A signing AI character with a blank face isn't just a slightly dull signer. It's actually making grammatical mistakes.
 A recent paper by Kazi Mahathir Rahman, CTO and co-founder of Talksign, and his coauthors, Naveed Imtiaz Nafis, Md. Farhan Sadik, Mohammad Al Rafi, and Mehedi Hasan Shahed, make the case for 3D representation in sign language translation. In their paper, Speak2Sign3D: A Multi-modal Pipeline for English Speech to American Sign Language Animation , they noted that ASL’s visual-spatial nature requires 3D models to capture facial cues, because 2D (text or flat video) often misses “subtle facial features and unique hand gestures essential for accuracy.” Their work starts from raw audio to preserve the tone, emphasis, and rhythm of the speaker’s voice, generating fluid 3D sign animation that reflects how sign language is actually used. This shift toward 3D is supported by the broader research community; foundational studies by Camgoz et al. (2020) and Saunders et al. (2020) have confirmed that we cannot treat sign language as a simple sequence of words, as 3D production is essential to capture fluid, natural movement. Furthermore, recent critiques by Yazdani et al. (2025) emphasize that text-based metrics fail to capture the complexity of signed languages, reinforcing that sign translation is fundamentally closer to robotics and computer vision than to plain text processing.
 The one-way problem
 Almost every accessibility system we use, whether at a stadium, on TV, or at work, only goes one way. The hearing person speaks or acts or the Deaf person reads or watches. Whatever the Deaf person signs back has no way to be understood unless a rare and expensive interpreter is there. A one-way channel isn't real communication; it's like a broadcast with a receiver.
 Palm , our sign-to-speech AI model, was made because we decided that going the other way was just as important from the start to achieve true two-way communication between a Deaf and Hearing person.
 The problem with how we show and use data for AI
 Sign language doesn't yet have a clear way for AI to understand it, like how text has words or pictures have pixels and it's not just about not having enough videos. How we show information affects what the AI learns. An AI model trained on words in a line will ignore information that happens all at once, and once that information is gone, you can't get it back. There are 300+ sign languages worldwide, each linguistically distinct, and no universal “sign alphabet” or text equivalent. In written languages we have letters or subword tokens; for signs, no agreed symbolic units exist. AI models can’t simply treat signs like text characters.
 Underneath this is a data problem that won't fix itself:
 There is much less sign language data than spoken language data. Training AI models usually requires vast datasets, but sign data sets are tiny in comparison to speech.
 A lot of the existing data was collected from Deaf communities without fair payment or permission, raising ethical and quality issues.
 Ways of checking how well a translation works, like counting how many words overlap, can make an AI model look good even if it produces something a native signer would say is wrong. Researchers have mentioned that text-based metrics fall short in capturing the multimodal complexity of sign language.
 That's why we built the Talksign Marketplace along with our AI models, so people who contribute, annotate data, and get paid for something that has historically been taken for free. And that's why having Deaf and hard-of-hearing people on our advisory board is a core rule, not just a nice gesture. You can't know if your grammar is correct if no one in the room understands the language natively.
 The wider impact: How better sign technology helps everyone
 Research into accessibility often ends up helping everyone. Captions now help people commuting or learning a new language, not just Deaf viewers. Speech recognition, which helps people with disabilities, is now on every phone. The same will likely happen where AI systems understand visual and language information and at the same time can be used in robots, augmented reality (AR), education, and working together remotely, far beyond just helping Deaf people. For example, we are building Talksign into AR glasses which allows real-time translation of speech or text displayed on your screen. We also see a future where a home assistant could respond to signed commands.
 A world beyond just captions
 Captions and human interpreters are some of the most important tools ever created for accessibility. They should keep getting better and be used more widely. The point is not that they are unnecessary. It is that they are not the complete answer. Captions are one way, interpreters can be expensive and difficult to access, and most everyday conversations still happen without either.
 Our research with the Deaf and signing communities has shown that while providing accessibility at big sports events, conferences, and TV shows is valuable and should absolutely be advocated for, it is not the same as building communication that works for everyday conversations, at every level, in both directions, without having to worry about the cost or wait for an interpreter.
 That’s been our focus building Talksign. We continue to work closely with the community to push the frontier of what our technology can do and build real-time, two-way communication between spoken and sign languages, enabling Deaf and hearing people to communicate instantly. Our goal is not simply to make individual conversations easier, but to expand access to education, healthcare, employment, public services, and everyday life, so that the ability to communicate is not determined by whether an interpreter is available.
 References
 Camgoz, N. C., et al. (2020). Sign Language Transformers: Joint End-to-end Sign Language Recognition and Translation . CVPR.
 Saunders, B., et al. (2020). Progressive Transformers for End-to-End Sign Language Production . ECCV.
 Yazdani, S., et al. (2025). A Critical Study of Automatic Evaluation in Sign Language Translation .

## Introducing the Talksign Marketplace
URL: https://www.talksign.co/blog/introducing-the-talksign-marketplace
Published: 25 Aug 2026 | Category: Product | Author: Edidiong Ekong, CEO and Founder of Talksign

A marketplace for licensable multimodal sign language datasets.

Today we're launching the Talksign Marketplace, a place where Deaf communities, researchers, institutions, and companies can contribute, annotate, license, and access high-quality sign language datasets. It's the missing infrastructure layer underneath every serious attempt to build AI that works for Deaf people, and it's the piece we've had to build ourselves in order to build anything else.
 The problem is data, and it always has been
 There are more than 430 million people worldwide with disabling hearing loss, and somewhere between 200 and 300 documented sign languages in active use. Almost none of them are represented in machine learning at anything close to the scale that spoken languages are.
 Watch on YouTube The Talksign Marketplace launch video, on our YouTube channel.
 Consider the asymmetry. A modern speech model trains on hundreds of thousands of hours of transcribed audio, scraped, licensed, and aggregated over two decades of open web infrastructure. The largest publicly available sign language corpora are measured in tens or low hundreds of hours, often recorded in a single studio, with a handful of signers, under controlled lighting, in one national sign language. The consequences show up everywhere downstream. Models trained on narrow corpora fail on regional variation, on Deaf-native signing rhythm, on the facial grammar that carries negation, questions, and intensity. They fail on anyone whose signing doesn't match the two dozen people in the training set. And because the failures are invisible to hearing evaluators reading BLEU scores, they get shipped anyway.
 Meanwhile the data that would fix this does exist. It sits in university archives with no licensing pathway, in Deaf organisations that recorded it for their own purposes, in the hands of individual signers who've never been offered a route to contribute on terms they'd accept. The bottleneck isn't that the data can't be created. It's that there's no market, no standard, and no mechanism that makes contributing worth anyone's time.
 Why this matters beyond translation
 It's tempting to read this as a narrow technical problem for a narrow set of companies. Sign languages are full natural languages with their own grammar, morphology, and syntax, and they're expressed simultaneously across the hands, the face, the upper body, and the use of space. Any model that handles them properly has to reason across several modalities at once, in real time, with meaning distributed across channels rather than sequenced in a line. That's a genuinely hard multimodal problem, and the field's inability to solve it well is partly an inability to get enough of the right data to try.
 The contributor app: signers pick paid briefs, upload clips and get paid.
 So the datasets that make bidirectional sign translation possible also happen to be some of the richest multimodal training material available anywhere. Contributing to this corpus isn't only an accessibility act. It advances the general problem of machine understanding embodied human communication.
 There's also a fairness argument we don't think should need making, but does. The Deaf community has spent decades as the subject of research it didn't control and didn't benefit from. Data was collected, papers were published, careers were built, and the communities who provided the raw material got a citation at best. If the next generation of accessibility AI is going to be trained on Deaf language, Deaf people should be paid for it and should have a say in how it's used.
 How the Marketplace works
 The Marketplace is built around four functions.
 Contribute: Individual signers, Deaf organisations, universities, and companies can submit recorded sign language data and receive payment for their contributions.
 Annotate: Raw video isn't training data. It becomes training data through gloss annotation, pose extraction, segmentation, and linguistic labelling, and that work is most accurate when it's done by fluent signers rather than outsourced to people who don't know the language. The Marketplace routes annotation work to the community and pays for it.
 License: Buyers get clear, machine-readable licence terms, provenance records, and dataset certificates. If you're building a product, you need to know where your training data came from and what you're allowed to do with it. If you're publishing research, you need to be able to state it. Right now most people building in this space genuinely cannot answer that question about their own corpora.
 Access: Researchers and startups can find, evaluate, and acquire datasets across languages, dialects, domains, and recording conditions in one place, instead of emailing thirty labs and waiting six months for a data use agreement.
 Verification, because trust can't be assumed
 Every dataset listed on the Marketplace is built to be checked through an open verification portal, so a buyer, a contributor, or an outside researcher can confirm what a dataset actually is before anyone builds on it. It's load-bearing, for a few reasons.
 Provenance: If you train a model on sign language data, you need to know where it came from and that the people in it agreed to be there. A marketplace without verifiable provenance just moves the consent problem around instead of solving it. The portal ties each dataset back to its source and its licence terms, so a claim of ethical sourcing is something you can check rather than something you have to take on faith.
 Consent and likeness rights: Sign language data is biometric by nature. It's a person's face, hands, and body carrying their language, and it can't be anonymised the way a text corpus can. That raises the stakes on getting consent right, and it means contributors deserve a durable record that their material is being used only under the terms they agreed to. Verification makes that record auditable on both sides.
 Quality and integrity: The value of a dataset depends on things a listing can assert but a buyer can't easily see: whether the annotations are accurate, whether the signers are fluent, whether the recording conditions match what's claimed, whether the file is what it says it is and hasn't been altered or duplicated from somewhere else. The portal lets those properties be confirmed independently, so quality is demonstrated rather than advertised.
 And there's a wider reason. A field that has historically treated Deaf language as free raw material doesn't earn trust back with promises. It earns it by making its claims checkable. Open verification is how we hold ourselves to the standard we're asking the rest of the industry to meet.
 What we've learned building Palm and Echo
 We didn't arrive at this from theory. Palm 1.0, our sign-to-speech model, was trained on over 71,000 samples and reaches 84.2% semantic accuracy. Echo 1.0, which turns speech into sign, is trained on 94,410 ASL sentence pairs, translates in roughly 29 milliseconds and hits 0.927 SSIM at 30 frames per second.
 Getting there meant assembling data ourselves, in partnership with Deaf communities, over a long period, at considerable cost. Every improvement in those numbers traced back to data quality and coverage rather than architecture. And every time we wanted to expand into a new sign language, we hit the same wall from the beginning.
 We're not the only team hitting that wall. We'd rather solve it once, in the open, than have every group in the field rebuild the same private corpus at the same expense and arrive at the same narrow coverage. The Marketplace is the version of that infrastructure we wish had existed when we started.
 Our position on this
 We build with Deaf communities, not for them. That principle has a specific implication for data, which is that community-sourced language material should generate ongoing value for the people who provided it, and those people should retain a say in how it's licensed and what it's used for. A marketplace is the honest structure for that. It makes the exchange visible and it makes the terms negotiable, rather than burying both inside a research consent form.
 We also think captions are not sufficient accessibility, and the data problem is one reason why. Captioning is what you build when you can only afford to solve one direction of the conversation. Bidirectionality, letting Deaf users respond in their own language and be understood, requires understanding sign language as language, and that requires a corpus that doesn't currently exist at the scale needed. The Marketplace is how it gets built.
 Getting involved
 The Marketplace is now live. If you hold sign language data and want to list it, if you're a signer or organisation interested in contributing or annotating, or if you're building something that needs licensed multimodal sign data, we'd like to hear from you. You can sign up on the Talksign Marketplace or reach us directly at sales@talksign.co .
 You can also read more about the models this work supports in our write-up of Palm and Echo , or book a demo .

## Introducing Palm 1.0 and Echo 1.0
URL: https://www.talksign.co/blog/palm-and-echo
Published: 22 May 2026 | Category: Research | Author: Edidiong Ekong, CEO and Founder of Talksign

Palm 1.0 and Echo 1.0 set a new global standard for real-time sign language translation with 84% semantic accuracy, delivering human-competitive accuracy and opening the door to a truly inclusive future.

Today, we are announcing the release of two new flagship models: Palm 1.0 and Echo 1.0 . Both succeed Talksign-1 and form the new engine powering the Talksign platform across mobile, desktop and web, with smart glasses planned.
 A defining moment in Sign Language history
 For decades, sign language translation has represented one of the most formidable unsolved challenges in artificial intelligence. Unlike spoken language, sign language is not linear. It is a rich, multi-dimensional system of communication in which the simultaneous positions of the hands, the orientation of the fingers, movement through space, and facial expression all combine to form meaning in a single instant. Teaching a machine to understand this language has, until now, remained an aspirational goal.
 At Talksign, a major part of our innovation and research has been focused on solving this.
 We are proud to announce Talksign Palm 1.0 , the Pose-Aligned Language Model, our flagship sign-to-text engine, and Talksign Echo 1.0 , our text-to-sign engine that generates photorealistic avatars and video in real time. Together, they take sign language AI across the threshold from research curiosity to production-ready deployment.
 Palm 1.0 and Echo 1.0 are the first models we are confident putting into the hands of Deaf users at scale. Talksign-1 proved the architecture worked. Palm and Echo prove it works well enough to ship. The next step is putting them everywhere a Deaf person needs to communicate. On a phone, on glasses, in a hospital, in a classroom.
 Edidiong Ekong, CEO and co-founder, Talksign
 Palm 1.0: Sign Language AI with true meaning and context
 The performance of an AI system must ultimately be judged by a simple question: Does it work well enough for real people, in the real world? By every established metric in the field of natural language processing and translation quality, Palm 1.0 answers that question with an emphatic yes.
 Palm 1.0 against the targets for production translation
 Semantic accuracy ROUGE Target 75% 84.2% Word-level accuracy BLEU-1 Target 70% 79.6% Phrase accuracy BLEU-4 Production-ready 30% 36.6% Target for each metric Trained At Scale Palm 1.0 was trained on over 71,000 samples, giving it a massive vocabulary of signs and conversational sentences drawn from real, diverse signers. 84.2% semantic accuracy: the meaning is understood
 Palm 1.0 achieves a ROUGE semantic accuracy score of 84.2%. This is the most critical of all translation metrics. It measures not whether the AI found the exact right word, but whether it captured the correct meaning. In more than four out of every five signing sequences, Palm 1.0 correctly understands what the signer is trying to say: the intent, the subject, the action, the context. To appreciate what this represents, consider that a human professional interpreter operating under real-time conditions in a noisy environment achieves semantic fidelity in a similar range. PALM 1.0 operates with zero fatigue, zero latency, and zero error variance across millions of simultaneous inferences.
 79.6% word-level accuracy: approaching human fluency
 At the word level, Palm 1.0 achieves a BLEU-1 score of 79.6%. This places the model in territory previously reserved only for mature, high-resource translation systems for Spanish, French, and Mandarin, languages with decades of training data and commercial investment. Palm 1.0 achieves near-equivalent word accuracy for a visual, spatial language that has historically lacked a fraction of that data infrastructure.
 36.6% BLEU-4: beyond research, into reality
 BLEU-4 is the most stringent standard in translation evaluation. A BLEU-4 score of 36.6% does not merely match the field. It exceeds published benchmarks from leading academic research institutions and reaches phrase-level accuracy at a scale that makes real-world deployment feasible. Machine translation systems for spoken languages are generally considered production-ready at BLEU-4 above 30%. Palm 1.0 clears that threshold by 6.6 points.
 Palm 1.0 against the field
 Palm 1.0 against the field
 Phrase accuracy BLEU-4 vs production-ready 30% 36.6% Phrase accuracy BLEU-4 vs academic state of the art ~28 to 32% 36.6% Word-level fluency BLEU-1 target 70% 79.6% Semantic preservation ROUGE target 75% 84.2% Benchmark standard Architecture: The SAGE Encoder-Decoder Transformer 
 Palm 1.0 is built on an Encoder-Decoder Transformer architecture with a proprietary mechanism at its core called SAGE (Spatial Attention Graph Encoder). 
 Most sign language models track body points in isolation. SAGE takes a different approach. It maps the human body as a connected graph of 133 anatomical landmarks and continuously tracks how those landmarks relate to each other in motion. The result is a model that does not just see where your hands are. It understands what your hands, head, and body are doing together, and what that combination means.
 This matters because sign language is not a sequence of isolated gestures. A hand shape means one thing in one context and something entirely different when paired with a particular head position or shoulder movement. SAGE captures those relationships in real time and passes that structural understanding to the decoder, so Palm 1.0 can read signing the way it is actually produced: as a continuous, contextual conversation.
 Echo 1.0: a Photorealistic Aperture Model for Sign Language
 Echo 1.0 is Talksign’s end-to-end pipeline for converting spoken or written language into photorealistic American Sign Language video at 30 frames per second. A person speaks or types, and Echo 1.0 outputs a high-fidelity digital human signing the equivalent message fluently and accurately.
 Talksign photorealistic avatars, signing with Echo 1.0.
 Trained At Scale Echo 1.0 was trained on 94,410 ASL sentence pairs over 15 epochs, producing a translation engine fluent in the syntax, word order, and spatial grammar that make ASL its own distinct language. Echo 1.0 at a glance
 0.927 Perceptual quality SSIM, above 0.90 reads as high quality ~29 ms Translation latency Per sample, across 5,000 examples 30 FPS Real-time video Photorealistic avatar output Visual quality that disappears into the signing
 Echo 1.0 achieves a Structural Similarity Index (SSIM) of 0.927 and a Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio of 29.5 dB on photorealistic rendering. An SSIM above 0.90 is widely accepted as indicating perceptually high quality. In practical terms, it means viewers stop noticing the rendering and focus on the signing itself, which is the only metric of visual quality that ultimately matters for accessibility. A complementary LPIPS perceptual loss score of 0.081 confirms that human viewers perceive the generated video as visually authentic rather than an obviously synthesized avatar.
 Translation latency under 30 milliseconds
 Echo 1.0’s translation stage runs at approximately 29 milliseconds per sample, measured across 5,000 validation examples. That latency is below the threshold of human perception for conversational delay, which is what makes the difference between a tool that feels real-time and a tool that feels like a transcription service. Combined with 30 frames-per-second video output at production-standard resolution, Echo 1.0 is the first text-to-sign system Talksign has shipped that can credibly support live, conversational use.
 Echo 1.0 under the hood
 ~29 ms Stage 1 translation Per sample, across 5,000 validation examples ~2.1 s Stage 2 rendering Per 100 inference steps 30 FPS Video output Production resolution, all major web and mobile formats 11 h 44 m Stage 1 training 15 epochs on 94,410 samples (cloud GPU) 6 h 2 m Stage 2 training 10,000 fine-tuning iterations on an NVIDIA T4 GPU Translating English into ASL, not transcribing it
 ASL isn’t English in another modality. It’s a different language with its own grammar, word order, and spatial syntax. Echo 1.0’s translation layer achieves a ROUGE semantic score of 58.4% and BLEU-1 word accuracy of 66.2% on English-to-ASL gloss translation, consistent with the current state of the art for this notoriously hard linguistic problem. The point isn’t the absolute number. It’s that Echo is solving the right problem. Most existing tools transcribe English word-for-word and call it sign language. Echo restructures English into ASL the way a fluent signer would.
 The three-step pipeline
 Echo 1.0 operates as a seamless three-stage process. From the moment a user speaks to the moment a signed video appears, the entire pipeline executes automatically.
 Speech recognition. Spoken audio is transcribed into written English using any industry-standard ASR system. The pipeline is modular, so any text source can feed directly into Step 2 without going through audio at all.
 Text to ASL gloss. Talksign’s proprietary neural translation layer converts English text into ASL gloss, preserving the grammar, word order, and spatial syntax of natural signing rather than producing a word-for-word English mapping.
 Gloss to photorealistic video. Each gloss token is matched to a high-fidelity 3D motion sequence and rendered by a photorealistic neural engine, animating a digital human with full-body movement, hand articulation, and facial expressions at 30 frames per second.
 One reference photo, one personalized avatar
 Echo 1.0 supports bespoke avatar customization. A custom signing presenter can be generated from a single reference image, with the underlying anatomy and motion system held constant.
 Modular by design
 Every stage of Echo 1.0 can be updated, replaced, or fine-tuned independently. As speech recognition, translation, and neural rendering each advance, Echo evolves with them without requiring a full system retrain.
 What this means for the world
 Numbers and architecture tell part of the story. The true significance of Palm 1.0 and Echo 1.0 is only visible when you consider who they serve and what they make possible for the first time.
 A world without communication barriers
 There are an estimated 430 million people worldwide with disabling hearing loss, and tens of millions more who use sign language as their primary or preferred language. For these individuals, the world has long presented unnecessary friction at every turn: in hospitals, courtrooms, classrooms, government offices, and everyday social interactions. Professional sign language interpreters are scarce, expensive, and unavailable in countless contexts where communication is urgent and necessary.
 Palm 1.0 and Echo 1.0 change the economics and logistics of this problem. A model that achieves 84% semantic accuracy, runs in real time, and operates on accessible hardware can serve as a universal communication bridge in contexts where human interpreters are absent. It can power accessibility features in video conferencing platforms, public service applications, educational tools, and healthcare systems, delivering understanding to the moments that matter most.
 The Deaf community: partners, not subjects
 At Talksign, we hold a foundational principle. Technology that serves the Deaf community must be built with the Deaf community. Palm 1.0 was trained on data that reflects the diversity, richness, and natural variation of real human signing, not a synthetic approximation. Echo 1.0’s motion dictionary was reviewed with Deaf advisors. As we move toward deployment, Talksign is committed to ongoing collaboration with Deaf advocates, linguists, and users to ensure that Palm and Echo continue to improve in the dimensions that matter most to those they serve. Accessibility is not a feature. It is the product.
 The next frontier: signing as a first-class interface
 Beyond accessibility, Palm and Echo open an entirely new frontier in human-computer interaction. For decades, the keyboard and the voice have been the dominant interfaces between humans and machines. Sign language, a natural, expressive, and physically intuitive mode of communication, has been left outside the circle of machine understanding.
 With Palm 1.0 and Echo 1.0, signing becomes a first-class interface. A world where a surgeon who cannot speak during a procedure can sign instructions to a clinical AI. Where a child born Deaf learns mathematics through an AI tutor that understands them naturally. Where any device, anywhere, can bridge the full spectrum of human communication without loss.
 Sign language is not linear text. It is spatial, temporal, and grammatical all at once. Palm’s dual stream architecture and Echo’s three-stage decoupling were both designed for that. The result is a stack where language, motion, and rendering can each be improved without retraining the others.
 Kazi Mahathir Rahman, co-founder and CTO, Talksign
 Known limitations of Echo 1.0
 Specialized vocabulary in domains like medicine, law, and engineering currently requires fine-tuning. Out of the box, Echo 1.0 is fluent in everyday and conversational ASL but isn’t yet calibrated for every technical domain.
 Each deployed avatar is fine-tuned to a specific identity. Switching between avatars within the same deployment requires a separate fine-tuning run.
 Output is reliably word-accurate but doesn’t always capture idiomatic, multi-word ASL phrasing. The expansion of training data planned for v1.1 aims to deliver a substantial lift here.
 Echo 1.0 currently accepts English input. Spanish, French, and Arabic input are scheduled for v1.1.
 Native video output is optimized for standard streaming resolution. Higher resolutions for broadcast and large-screen deployment will be supported natively in v1.1.
 Sign sequences are produced by concatenating individual signs. Natural co-articulation and signing prosody are approximated rather than fully modeled, and are a primary focus for v1.1.
 On the roadmap
 Multi-language input: Spanish, French, and Arabic speech and text alongside English, extending Echo to a much wider speaking audience.
 Additional sign languages: British Sign Language (BSL), Deutsche Gebärdensprache (DGS), and Nigerian Sign Language, with the long-term goal of supporting every national sign language in the world.
 Larger training corpus: expansion of Echo’s text-to-gloss corpus from 94,000 to more than 500,000 ASL sentence pairs, targeting native idiomatic accuracy.
 Universal avatar model: dynamic identity switching at inference time, removing the need for per-subject fine-tuning.
 Higher resolution output: native 1024×1024 rendering and beyond, for broadcast and large-screen use.
 Real-time streaming: continuous frame delivery for live captioning, with on-device inference bringing Palm and Echo to phones, browsers, and smart glasses without round-trips to the cloud.
 Domain modules: plug-in vocabulary packs for healthcare, education, legal, and public-service contexts.
 Enterprise APIs: direct embedding in Zoom, Teams, Netflix, EHR systems, LMS platforms, and any product where communication happens.
 Availability
 Palm 1.0 and Echo 1.0 will be publicly available across the Talksign web app and mobile and desktop apps from August 20, 2026. Support for Meta Ray-Ban smart glasses is planned for early 2027.
 Ahead of general availability, we're recruiting pilot partners across healthcare, education, Deaf organizations, NGOs, enterprise, and airports. If you or your organization wants early access, sign our Letter of Intent 
 About Talksign
 Talksign is an AI accessibility company building real-time, bidirectional translation between spoken and sign languages across smart glasses, mobile, desktop, and the web. The company’s mission is simple. No one should be left out of a conversation. Talksign is built with, not for, the Deaf community, with datasets and models co-designed with Deaf users, educators, and researchers.

## Introducing Talksign-1
URL: https://www.talksign.co/blog/introducing-talksign-1
Published: 16 Feb 2026 | Category: Research | Author: Edidiong Ekong, CEO and Founder of Talksign

Breaking down communication barriers with our first-generation AI model for real-time Sign Language recognition

Today, we're excited to announce Talksign-1, our foundation model for sign language understanding. This represents a significant step forward in making communication truly accessible for the Deaf and hard-of-hearing community, offering real-time, accurate translation between sign language and speech.
 Why we built Talksign-1
 Over 70 million people worldwide use sign language as their primary mode of communication. Yet most digital tools, from video conferencing to customer service kiosks, still assume everyone can speak and hear. The gap isn't just inconvenient; it's a barrier to participation in everyday life.
 We built Talksign-1 to close that gap. It's purpose-built for real-time bidirectional translation between sign language and speech.
 Two modes, one model
 Sign‑to‑Speech. Talksign-1 processes MediaPipe landmark sequences from a standard webcam and classifies them against a vocabulary of 250 ASL signs. Predictions return with confidence scores in under 100ms at p95.
 Speech‑to‑Sign. Spoken or typed speech is sent to our Speech2Sign engine, which returns an ordered sequence of sign language video clips with optional 3D avatar animation data for future rendering.
 Real-time inference. Talksign-1 buffers 30 frames of landmark data before predicting, balancing temporal coverage with low latency. Combined with motion-aware gating, it only infers when meaningful signing is detected.
 Browser-native. Talksign-1 inference runs on the server side behind a single unified API. Everything works in a standard web browser.
 Performance
 Talksign-1 is a real-time sign‑to‑text AI model that converts American Sign Language into speech/text from live camera input using 3D body, hand, and face landmarks extracted with MediaPipe, rather than raw video. It’s built in TensorFlow/Keras as a transformer‑enhanced CNN, trained on a large‑scale ASL dataset (WLASL2000) to recognize a focused vocabulary of everyday signs. During use, Talksign-1 buffers short motion sequences (about a second of signing), analyzes spatiotemporal patterns, and outputs the most likely gloss with a confidence score. This powers Talksign’s real‑time sign‑to‑text experience in the browser. Here are the benchmarks on a held-out validation/test set:
 Talksign-1 on a held-out validation and test set
 ~68 to 74% Top-1 accuracy Correct sign as the first guess ~85 to 90% Top-5 accuracy Correct sign in the top five ~40 to 60 ms Inference latency p50, and ~100 to 150 ms at p95 250 Sign vocabulary Everyday ASL signs These numbers reflect isolated sign recognition: discrete glosses, not continuous sentence-level interpretation. For many real-world use cases (quick greetings, common requests, basic conversation), this vocabulary covers significant ground. We're actively expanding it.
 Impact
 The technology is designed for inclusion across multiple use cases:
 Education . Students and teachers communicate in real time through sign language translation, creating more engaging, inclusive classrooms and equal access to learning.
 Healthcare . Clear, direct communication between patients and providers improves understanding, diagnosis, and care without waiting for interpreters.
 Workplace . Participate fully in meetings, collaborate with colleagues, and access HR and compliance information via real-time speech-to-text and sign-to-text translation.
 Public Spaces . Transport announcements, emergency alerts, and public information are translated instantly into sign language on personal devices and digital displays.
 Broadcasting . Live news, entertainment, and emergency updates delivered with on-screen sign language avatars for accessible viewing.
 Safety & Emergency Response . You can integrate Talksign with CCTV and safety systems to enable faster emergency response and better protection for deaf and hard-of-hearing communities.
 Deployment
 The entire Talksign platform: frontend, backend, and both AI engines run on a single EC2 instance orchestrated with Docker Compose behind Nginx with TLS termination. Model weights are loaded from the local file system at startup. There is no dependency on S3 or external model hosting in the current deployment.
 Each AI service (sign2speech, speech2sign) is an independent container that can be scaled vertically by increasing instance resources or horizontally by adding more nodes. The architecture is designed to evolve without changing the frontend contract.
 Limitations and responsible use
 Talksign-1 is an early-stage model, and we want to be transparent about what it can and cannot do today.
 Vocabulary. Talksign-1 recognizes 250 signs. Out-of-vocabulary signs, fingerspelling, and continuous sentence-level signing are not supported in this release. Performance may degrade with unusual lighting, camera angles, or signing styles outside the training distribution.
 Scope. The model is designed for isolated sign recognition: discrete glosses, not grammatical interpretation of full ASL sentences. It should not be used as a sole authority in medical, legal, or safety-critical settings without human oversight.
 Privacy. Landmark extraction happens client-side in the browser. Only processed keypoint data, not raw video, is sent to the server. User data is handled in accordance with the Talksign privacy policy.
 We believe AI should augment, not replace, human interpreters. Talksign-1 is built to support communication and accessibility in everyday situations, and we're committed to expanding its capabilities responsibly.
 Our commitment to the Deaf community
 Talksign-1 wasn't built in isolation. We've partnered with Deaf educators, native ASL signers, and accessibility advocates throughout the development process. The WLASL2000 dataset reflects the diversity and richness of real sign language, and our model respects that complexity.
 We believe accessibility is a human right, not a feature. Talksign-1 is our contribution to a world where communication barriers no longer separate people.
 What's next
 We're already working on the next generation of TS models with larger vocabularies, continuous sentence recognition, support for fingerspelling, and multi-sign language coverage (BSL, LSF, and others). Talksign-1 is the foundation. We can't wait to show you what comes next.
 Try Talksign-1 today
 Talksign-1 is now live in the app at talksign.co . Open the app, allow camera and microphone access, and start translating in either direction.
